summary:
No department-level trans statute, ordinance, enforcement finding or incident series for Junín appears in the inventory, so the department stands under Peru's national framework and the national assessment governs what a trans visitor to Junín should expect. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The restroom restriction moved through Congress in two steps. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody situations, where medical attention is required, or when accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and with a parallel ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The immediate trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the fused text, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject only to narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement rests on private judgment at the door. Activist Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 hate-crime report, warns that access would come down to security staff assessing identity documents on their own discretion, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The legal analysis of Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte at IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The restriction reaches private and public life alike. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI recorded 54 murders of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, including 12 trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty such as multiple gunshots and stabbings; the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints in 2020 alone. The inventory recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2024 report co-authored by Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and she stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Impunity has been broken once. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The absence of hate-crime protection is a matter of record. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between the national law and international standards is the central turbulence in the record. The Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 protects gender identity as personal autonomy, while the April 2025 Peruvian statute does the opposite at the restroom door, and IDEHPUCP's analysis measures the statute against both the Peruvian Constitution and the American Convention on Human Rights.

Regional comparison is unusually sharp on hate-crime coverage. Peru sits with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American countries whose hate-crime provisions carry no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage after the 2017 repeal.

Public discourse around the restriction has been openly hostile. Congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons on the floor of Congress, and television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told congresswoman Susel Paredes to 'go use the men's room'. The bills themselves originated in a July 2023 social-media complaint about restroom labelling at Jorge Chávez airport.

The national figures have no department-level breakdown in the inventory, so the direction of travel for Junín rests on the national series: 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights violations in 2020-2023, 30 of the homicide victims trans women, with the annual homicide count rising from 13 in 2022 to 19 in 2023. Camacho's caution that the published counts are a sub-registry means the true level is higher than the record shows.
localsOnly:
Residents of Junín live under the national restroom statute rather than any departmental ordinance, so everyday access to public facilities, gyms, workplaces and shopping centres is governed by article 5 and by the individual judgment of security staff, who may demand identity documents. The dismissed gym complaint shows that a private business enforcing the rule has, so far, faced no successful consumer-protection challenge.

Healthcare access improved on paper in June 2024, when national health authorities struck pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, giving trans patients in Junín a documented basis for dignity-respecting treatment.

Constitutional litigation remains an available route for residents: an activist challenge produced a July 2025 ruling from a Lima constitutional court striking down an anti-equality decree, and IDEHPUCP at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru continues to publish the constitutional analysis that underpins such challenges.

Reporting and documentation channels exist but undercount. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI compiles the national homicide and rights-violation series, and its co-author Gianna Camacho states that the figures are only a sub-registry, so local incidents may go unrecorded unless they reach that observatory or a formal complaint.

Legal exposure for residents includes the heightened obscenity minimum of four years under the April 2025 law and the article 4 ban on media and advertising content, which Human Rights Watch identifies as a pretext for repression of trans-related material.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Junín-specific data on homicides, rights violations, police conduct, or restroom-policy enforcement, so the department's actual incidence of anti-trans violence is unresolved rather than assessed as low.

Whether article 5 has been applied in practice in Junín, by which institutions, and with what outcomes is not sourced; the only enforcement example in the record is the national dismissal of a complaint against a gym, whose location is not stated.

The entry, visa and document-presentation position for trans travellers arriving in Peru, including how gender markers on passports are treated at Peruvian border control, is not covered by any source in the inventory.

Whether the April 2025 law has been challenged before the Constitutional Court or is subject to interim suspension in Junín is unresolved; the only constitutional ruling on record, in July 2025, concerned a different anti-equality decree and was issued in Lima.

No source gives a breakdown of the 54 homicides or 170 violation cases by department, so no regional deviation from the national pattern can be confirmed or excluded.
